newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rouge killed German biker in 1994.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge killed German biker in 1994.

text.p: Dissident Khmer Rouge leader Ieng Sary on Monday handed over the remains of German Matthias Wolf in a plastic bag to a representative of the Order of Malta's Bangkok mission, witnesses said.

Ieng Sary, who was Khmer Rouge foreign minister during Pol Pot's brutal 1975-79 rule, said the 32-year-old Wolf had been executed and his remains burnt after he crossed into the mountainous Phnom Malai area from Thailand.
Wolf, then 32, was last seen in the Thai border village of Ban Laem on December 8, 1994, before he crossed into northwest Cambodia's Phnom Malai region on his motorcycle.

The remains of the young German were handed to Jacques Bekaert of the Maltese Order. Ieng Sary told reporters Wolf had been killed in the Veal Veng area on the orders of Khmer Rouge defence chief Son Sen.
Bekaert, a Belgian national who has also followed the Cambodian story for several years as a journalist, said he received the remains on behalf of the German Embassy in Bangkok.

Ieng Sary broke away with Khmer Rouge hardliners loyal to Pol Pot in early August and since has been negotiating a reconciliation with the Cambodia government. He agreed at peace talks last week to recognise Phnom Penh's authority.
The breakaway faction leader said Wolf was shot by his captors on December 16, 1994, and petrol was poured over his body and set alight.
"It was very savage," said Ieng Sary, who added that nobody would have dared kill foreign hostages of the Khmer Rouge without orders from Pol Pot.

A Cambodian army officer had told reporters earlier in the northwest city of Battambang that guerrillas in Malai claimed Ieng Sary had not known about the killing of Wolf at the time as he was in Thailand receiving medical treatment.
Ieng Sary and Pol Pot were in 1979 sentenced to death in absentia for their roles in the genocide of more than one million people in the "killing fields" rule of the Khmer Rouge in the late 1970s.
The Khmer Rouge signed a peace accord in 1991, but later reneged on the accord and have been fighting the coalition government that emerged from United Nations-run elections in 1993.
The guerrillas have abducted several Westerners since resuming their struggle against the central government in 1993, releasing a handful and killing at least six besides Wolf.

The Bangkok Post reported on August 30 that British mine clearance expert Christopher Howes, who was kidnapped with his interpreter, Houn Hourth, in late March, had been executed a day earlier by guerrillas in northern Cambodia.
Khmer Rouge radio, which has kept up a daily dose of invective against Ieng Sary and his followers since early August, denied the report.
